description: We are building a web application to help users plan safer Mars exploration routes. By turning complex mission data into an interactive experience, users can compare paths while managing oxygen, time, radiation, dust, and communication constraints. Our goal is to show how software can improve decision-making for future Mars missions while making space science engaging and understandable.
summary:
Valles is a dual-mode Martian exploration platform built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It addresses the challenge of making Extravehicular Activity (EVA) planning both scientifically rigorous and publicly accessible through two products sharing one computational core: Mars Survival, a narrative-driven 3D survival game across five authentic Martian regions, and Mission Planner, a professional-grade EVA decision-support tool with multi-profile route optimization and automated safety validation.

What makes Valles distinctive is its responsible AI architecture — the Strict Semantic Split — where Google Gemini 3.6 Flash is strictly restricted to parsing natural language intent, while 100% of environmental values (temperature, pressure, dust opacity, radiation) are sourced directly from NASA’s Curiosity rover REMS dataset. This prevents AI hallucination in a safety-critical context. By grounding generative AI in empirical NASA data and pairing it with an A* pathfinder and NASA PLSS metabolic model, Valles proves that rigorous space science and engaging public software are not mutually exclusive.
details:
What it does:
Valles operates as two interconnected products on a shared physics engine. Mars Survival guides users through 14 story missions across Jezero Crater, Valles Marineris, Olympus Mons, Arcadia Planitia, and Hellas Basin, with real 0.38g low-gravity mechanics, live resource telemetry (O₂, battery, thermal load, suit integrity), and Earth communications delays of 3–22 minutes simulating actual orbital propagation lag. Mission Planner provides four traverse optimization profiles (Fastest, Safest, Balanced, Planner Default), automated Point-of-No-Return validation at every waypoint with a mandatory 10% oxygen safety margin, and NASA REMS-grounded mission briefings generated by Gemini 2.5 Flash.

How it works:
The core engine is built in TypeScript and comprises four modules: an A* pathfinder with a binary min-heap on an 8-connected elevation grid; a multi-criteria cost function weighting slope (normalized as S/90), surface roughness, hazard intensity, radiation exposure, and communications gap; a NASA PLSS-calibrated metabolic simulator modeling grade-dependent oxygen consumption and rover battery drain; and a shelter reachability checker that flags unsafe waypoints in real time. On top of this, a FastAPI backend handles natural language parsing via Gemini 2.5 Flash and REMS data lookup, enforcing the Strict Semantic Split — Gemini extracts intent only, the REMS engine supplies all numerical values, and Gemini then writes the mission briefing exclusively from those confirmed figures.

Benefits and intended impact:
For students and the public, Valles provides an intuitive, physics-grounded entry point into planetary science and EVA risk — something no existing tool offers without sacrificing accuracy. For mission designers and researchers, it provides a functional prototype for the kind of autonomous EVA decision-support systems that crewed Mars missions will require, particularly given the 3–22 minute Earth communication delay that makes real-time Houston support impossible on Mars.

Tools, languages, and technologies used:

  • Frontend: React 18, Vite, TypeScript, Three.js, Framer Motion, Recharts, MapLibre
  • Backend: Python 3.10+, FastAPI, Pydantic v2, Google Gemini 2.5 Flash API
  • Database & Infrastructure: Supabase (PostgreSQL, 12 tables, Row-Level Security, Auth), Deno Edge Functions for weekly challenge rotation
  • Data: NASA MSL Curiosity REMS MODRDR v1.0 archive, synthetic MOLA-referenced elevation matrices for 5 Martian regions
  • Testing: Vitest (30-case engine test suite)
  • License: MIT open source

Creativity and design considerations:
The team’s core creative decision was refusing to build two separate products. The same A* pathfinder and metabolic simulator that powers a student’s survival mission also validates a mission planner’s EVA route — ensuring that scientific fidelity is never traded for accessibility. The Strict Semantic Split is an original architectural pattern developed specifically for this project to solve the hallucination problem in mission-critical AI tools. Every environmental telemetry value displayed in the UI is traceable to a peer-reviewed scientific paper, with inline citations accessible to users.
